summary: Bilateral BGP sessions between exchange participants have long been the norm, but the overhead of managing many of them has made route servers popular. This informational document describes operational considerations for running and using route servers at Internet Exchange Points. It complements the route server specification.

plainLanguage.summary: An Internet exchange is a place where networks connect with each other. This document explains the machine many exchanges now use to share routing information instead of wiring every participant to every other one, and the care an operator has to take to keep it safe and reliable.

questions: how to operate an ixp route server
how do route servers reduce bgp sessions
subtitle: How an Internet exchange runs BGP route servers, and what the operator has to watch out for.

tldr.problem: At an Internet exchange, each participant that wants an open policy has to peer with every other participant, and the number of sessions grows as the square of the number of routers, with the configuration work to match.
tldr.mechanism: A route server sits in the middle, takes BGP routes from its clients and redistributes them to the other clients under a policy, leaving the NEXT_HOP attribute untouched so traffic still flows directly between the participants.
tldr.outcome: Each router then needs one session instead of many, and the sessions fall from n*(n-1)/2 to n, at the cost of new failure modes that the document works through: path hiding, scaling limits, prefix leaks and NEXT_HOP hijacking.

today: RFC 7948 is an Informational document published in September 2016. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it complements rather than replaces the route server specification in RFC 7947, which defines how the route server itself behaves.

sections.title: Why Exchanges Use Route Servers
sections.content:
Internet Exchange Points provide IP data interconnection facilities for their participants, using data link-layer protocols such as Ethernet. The Border Gateway Protocol is normally used to exchange network reachability information over these media.

Bilateral interconnection means interconnecting routers using individual BGP sessions between each pair of participant routers. If an IXP participant wishes to implement an open interconnection policy, a policy of interconnecting with as many other participants as possible, it has to liaise with each of its intended interconnection partners, and a BGP session is configured on both routers. If every participant interconnects with every other participant, a full mesh of BGP sessions is needed.

The number of BGP sessions at an exchange has an upper bound of n*(n-1)/2, where n is the number of routers at the exchange. Since many exchanges have large numbers of participating networks, the administrative and operational overhead needed for an open interconnection scales quadratically. New participants need significant initial resourcing before they get value from their connection, and existing participants have to commit ongoing resources to interconnect with each new one.

Multilateral interconnection is implemented using a route server configured to distribute BGP routes among client routers. A route server redistributes the BGP routes it receives from its clients to other clients according to a prespecified policy, and it can be viewed as similar to an EBGP equivalent of an IBGP route reflector.
sections.plainLanguage: If every network at an exchange wants to reach every other network, each pair needs its own BGP session. With twenty routers that is a hundred and ninety sessions, and every new router means a session on every existing router. A route server replaces all of that with one session per router.

sections.title: How a Route Server Works
sections.content:
The route server preserves the BGP NEXT_HOP attribute from all the routes it receives and passes them on with an unchanged NEXT_HOP to its clients, according to its configured routing policy. Using this method, an IXP participant router can receive an aggregated list of BGP routes from all the other route server clients using a single BGP session to the route server, instead of depending on BGP sessions with every router at the exchange. This reduces the overall number of BGP sessions at an exchange from n*(n-1)/2 to n, where n is the number of routers at the exchange.

Although a route server uses BGP to exchange reachability information with each of its clients, it does not forward traffic itself and is therefore not a router. In practice this allows dense interconnection between participants with low administrative overhead and significantly simpler and smaller router configurations. New participants benefit from immediate and extensive interconnection, and existing route server participants receive reachability information from these new participants without necessarily having to modify their configurations.

Multilateral and bilateral interconnections are not exclusive, and it is not unusual to have both sorts of session configured in parallel at an IXP. That configuration leads to additional paths being available to the BGP Decision Process, which calculates a best path as normal.
sections.plainLanguage: The route server passes routes on without changing where they point. It never carries the traffic itself, so a call or a connection still goes directly from one participant to another. The route server only decides which routes each client is allowed to hear about.

sections.title: Path Hiding and Per-Client Policies
sections.content:
Path hiding is the process whereby a route server masks individual paths by applying conflicting routing policies to its Loc-RIB. When this happens, route server clients receive incomplete information from the route server about network reachability.

Several approaches exist to mitigate the effect of path hiding. However, the only method that does not require explicit support from the route server client is for the route server itself to maintain an individual Loc-RIB for each client that is the subject of conflicting routing policies.

The price of that approach is computing resources. Because the BGP Decision Process has to be applied to all Loc-RIBs deployed on the route server, both CPU and memory requirements scale approximately according to O(P * N), where P is the total number of unique paths received by the route server and N is the number of clients that require a unique Loc-RIB. Because this is a super-linear relationship, large route servers may benefit from deploying per-client Loc-RIBs only where they are required.
sections.plainLanguage: If two clients get different sets of routes, one of them cannot see paths that exist. The fix is to give each client its own routing table on the route server, and that fix costs processor time and memory, so it is worth doing only for the clients that need it.

sections.title: Scaling: What Becomes Expensive
sections.content:
Regardless of whether any Loc-RIB optimization technique is implemented, the route server's theoretical upper-bound network bandwidth requirements scale according to O(P_tot * N), where P_tot is the total number of unique paths received by the route server and N is the total number of route server clients. If the average number of unique paths received per client, P_avg, stays roughly constant as the number of connected clients increases, then the total number of prefixes equals the average number of prefixes multiplied by the number of clients, which is written as P_tot = P_avg * N. Assuming the worst case, where each prefix is associated with a different set of BGP path attributes and so must be transmitted individually, the bandwidth scaling function becomes O((P_avg * N) * N), or O(N^2). This quadratic upper bound indicates that the route server model may not scale well for larger numbers of clients.

In practice, most prefixes are associated with a limited number of BGP path attribute sets, which allows more efficient transmission than the theoretical analysis suggests. P_tot will increase monotonically with the number of clients but has an upper limit of the size of the full default-free routing table of the network in which the IXP is located. Observations from production route servers show that most clients generally avoid using custom routing policies, and so the route server may not need per-client Loc-RIBs at all. These practical bounds reduce the theoretical worst case to the point where route server deployments are manageable even on larger IXPs.

The scaling analysis points to three practical challenges: route processor CPU overhead for BGP Decision Process calculations, memory for handling many different BGP path entries, and network bandwidth for distributing routes to each client. Three techniques are described for the first two.

View merging and decomposition optimises memory and CPU where multiple clients are subject to exactly the same routing policies: several Loc-RIB views can be merged into one. If the operator has prior knowledge of interconnection relationships, it can configure separate Loc-RIBs only for clients with unique policies, which requires each client to share its policies, in an internal provisioning database or in an external data store such as an Internet Routing Registry Database. Alternatively the implementation can create virtual Loc-RIBs from a single in-memory master Loc-RIB, with delta differences for each prefix subject to different policies, which is more fine-grained but needs a more complex in-memory structure. Whatever method is chosen, pathological edge cases can scale no better than fully non-optimized per-client Loc-RIBs.

Destination splitting has clients connect to multiple route servers and send non-overlapping sets of prefixes to each. Each route server computes the best path for its own set, so the quadratic requirement operates on smaller sets. In practice the operator would need every client to send a full set of routes to each route server and then filter selectively, using BGP Outbound Route Filtering or inbound prefix filters configured on the client sessions.

NEXT_HOP resolution can be simplified. Route servers are usually deployed at IXPs where all connected routers are on the same Layer 2 broadcast domain, so recursive resolution of the NEXT_HOP attribute is generally not required and can be replaced by a simple check that the NEXT_HOP value for each received route is a network address in the IXP LAN's IP address range.
sections.plainLanguage: The model gets expensive as more clients join, and the worst case is traffic growing with the square of the client count. In practice it is smaller, because most clients use the same rules and most prefixes share the same path attributes. Three techniques exist for the processor and memory side: share one table between clients with identical rules, split prefixes across several route servers, and skip the full next-hop lookup.

sections.title: Leaks, Redundancy and Next-Hop Hijacking
sections.content:
Prefix leakage mitigation. Prefix leakage occurs when a BGP client unintentionally distributes BGP routes to neighbouring BGP routers. Leakage to a route server can cause serious connectivity problems at an IXP if each client is configured to accept all routes from the route server. Because of the potential for collateral damage, route server operators are recommended to deploy prefix leakage mitigation measures to prevent unintentional announcements or else limit the scale of any such leak. Per-client inbound prefix limits can restrict the damage in many cases, though they are not foolproof; per-client inbound prefix filtering is a more deterministic and usually more reliable means, but requires more administrative resources to maintain. Where per-client filtering is implemented, the operator is also recommended to build in mechanisms that automatically compare the Adj-RIB-In received from each client with the inbound prefix lists configured for those clients. Many network operators do not carefully manage their published routing policies, and it is not uncommon to see significant variation between the two sets of prefixes.

Redundancy. Because the purpose of an IXP route server is to provide a reliable reachability brokerage service, it is recommended that operators provision multiple route servers on each shared Layer 2 domain. There is no requirement to use the same implementation or operating system for each, but where more than one server is provisioned on the same shared Layer 2 domain, each should be configured equivalently so that the path reachability information from each system is identical.

AS_PATH consistency check. BGP requires every speaker that advertises a route to an external speaker to prepend its own AS number as the last element of the AS_PATH, so the leftmost AS in an AS_PATH should equal the AS number of the speaker that sent the route. Because route servers are not supposed to modify the AS_PATH, a consistency check on the AS_PATH of a route received by a route server client would normally fail, and clients are recommended to disable that check towards the route server.

Export routing policies. A route server export policy affects prefixes sent from the route server to a client. Prefixes sent to the route server are commonly tagged with standard BGP Communities or Extended Communities values agreed between the operator and all clients, and the routes may then be propagated to all other clients, a subset, or none, which lets clients instruct the operator to implement per-client export policies. Because both standard and Extended Communities values are restricted to 6 octets or fewer, it is not possible for both the global and local administrator fields to fit a 4-octet AS number, so the operator should take care that the communities mechanism used is compatible with 4-octet AS numbers. Alternatively, Internet Routing Registry databases can be used to construct per-client policies, with RPSL providing a grammar for describing interconnection relationships and tools existing to translate it into route server configurations. An operator who wants neither may run its own policy database, which should allow a client to update its routing policy and to specify whether it wishes to exchange all its prefixes with any other client.

Layer 2 reachability. Ethernet switch forwarding bugs have occasionally been observed to cause non-transitive reachability: if two participants can reach the route server but cannot reach each other, traffic between them may be dropped until the Layer 2 forwarding problem is resolved. This does not tend to happen with bilateral interconnection, where the routing control path between two hosts is usually the same as the data path. Bidirectional Forwarding Detection can partly mitigate the problem, but there is currently no protocol to configure BFD sessions automatically between route server clients, and if two clients did run BFD between each other and detected a non-transitive loss of reachability, each would mark the other's prefixes as unreachable via the route server's path, which could cause sub-optimal routing or complete connectivity loss if there were no alternative paths.

NEXT_HOP hijacking. The rule that lets an external BGP speaker change the NEXT_HOP address of a received route to a different address on the same subnet is what allows route servers to operate on a shared Layer 2 IXP network, and it can be abused to redirect traffic for a client's prefixes to another IXP participant's router. If AS1 and AS2 both announce routes for AS99, AS1 could set the NEXT_HOP address for AS99's routes to the address of AS2's router, diverting traffic for AS99 via AS2 and overriding the routing policies of AS99 and AS2. Worse, if the operator does not use inbound prefix filtering, AS1 could announce any arbitrary prefix with the NEXT_HOP address of any other participant, which could be used as a denial-of-service mechanism. The problem is not specific to route servers and can also be implemented with bilateral BGP sessions, but the potential damage is amplified because a single BGP session can affect many networks at once. Because clients cannot easily implement next-hop policy checks against route server sessions, the operator should check that the NEXT_HOP attribute for routes received from a client matches that client's interface address, and SHOULD drop the route where the addresses differ and the announcing client is in a different AS from the client that uses the next-hop address. Permitting next-hop rewriting within the same AS lets an organisation with several connections into an IXP direct traffic off the IXP infrastructure through any of them.
sections.plainLanguage: The operator has a long checklist. Filter what each client is allowed to announce, so one mistake cannot black out the whole exchange. Run more than one route server, configured to agree. Turn off the path check that route servers would otherwise fail. Set the routing rules with communities, with the routing registries, or with a database of your own. Watch the switching fabric, because participants that can reach the route server but not each other will lose traffic between them. And check the next-hop address on every route, because otherwise one participant can point another participant's traffic at a third router.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
On route server installations that do not employ path-hiding mitigation techniques, the path-hiding problem could be used by an IXP participant to prevent the route server from sending any BGP routes for a particular prefix to other clients, even where a valid path existed via another client. That is, one participant could silence a destination for everyone else.

If the route server operator does not implement prefix leakage mitigation, it is trivial for clients to carry out denial-of-service attacks against arbitrary Internet networks by leaking BGP routes to a route server. Route server installations should be secured against BGP NEXT_HOP hijacking.
sections.plainLanguage: Two of the problems are useful to an attacker. One client can hide a destination from everyone else, and one client can flood the route server with routes for someone else's address space. Filtering what clients announce and checking the next-hop address close both of those.

items.title: CPU and memory
items.text: Both scale about O(P * N), where P is the unique paths received and N the clients needing their own Loc-RIB.

items.title: Network bandwidth
items.text: Scales O(P_tot * N), and in the worst case O(N^2), so the model may not scale well for larger numbers of clients.

items.title: Three levers
items.text: Merging views for clients with the same rules, splitting prefixes across several route servers, and simplifying the NEXT_HOP check.

items.title: What keeps it manageable
items.text: Most prefixes share a limited number of path attribute sets, and most clients avoid custom routing policies.

items.title: Filter what clients announce
items.text: Per-client inbound prefix filtering, checked against what each client actually sends.

items.title: Run more than one route server
items.text: Multiple route servers on each shared Layer 2 domain, configured so their paths are identical.

items.title: Disable the AS_PATH check
items.text: Clients should turn off the AS_PATH consistency check towards the route server.

items.title: Check the NEXT_HOP address
items.text: The operator should verify the NEXT_HOP matches the client's interface address, and drop the route when it does not.
